## Six of what? {#six-of-what .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Discuss with a neighbour · 2 minutes</p>
<p class="eyebrow">A report from the lab</p>
<p class="opening-report compact">“We treated cells with compound Q.<br>We measured enzyme activity.<br>n = 6 replicates.”</p>
<p class="takeaway keyline">What could “6 replicates” mean?</p>
<div class="triplicate-options fragment">
<p>Six readings of one sample?</p>
<p>Six cultures from one passage, treated on the same day?</p>
<p>Six separately initiated preparations, on different days?</p>
</div>

::: notes
**Time: 00:00–00:06 (6 minutes).**

**Say:** Open with the report on screen and nothing else. It is an incomplete fictional lab report, worded the way a methods section or figure legend typically reads. Do not supply a cell line, dose, time, control, plot or protocol yet. Ask what "6 replicates" could mean and give pairs two minutes to propose at least two meanings. Then advance once to show three possibilities and use two minutes to hear what information would distinguish them. All three are common uses of the word. Do not say which one applies, introduce technical vocabulary or ask for a numerical N. The next slide provides the first notebook detail.

**Context (not yet revealed):** L1 is a human cell line stably expressing kinase Q. Compound Q is a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor of kinase Q. The assay measures kinase Q activity (substrate phosphorylation rate, U/mg protein). These details are revealed progressively from the next slide onward.

**Conceptual point:** The word "replicates" does not identify what was repeated. Six readings of one sample share everything; six preparations on different days share much less. Different meanings support different claims.

**Likely misconception:** "Replicates" unambiguously means six independent experiments. In practice the word is used for anything from repeated readings or separate wells to separate experiment days.

**Optional follow-up:** What single question would you ask the person who did the experiment?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 17, 73–74, 121–122; R p. 13. New fictional wording; adapted ambiguity exercise.
:::

## What exactly did we do? {#what-did-we-do}

<p class="small">First notebook detail: one preparation of cell line L1 — a human cell line stably expressing kinase Q</p>
<div class="workflow" role="group" aria-label="One preparation followed through treatment and measurement">
<div class="stage"><div class="prep">P1</div><p>One culture<br>preparation</p></div>
<div class="connector"></div>
<div class="stage"><div class="tubes"><div class="tube v">V</div><div class="tube q">Q</div></div><p class="small">Split into two tubes<br>Randomly assign V or Q</p></div>
<div class="connector fragment" data-fragment-index="0"></div>
<div class="stage fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><div class="reading-row"><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i></div><div class="reading-row"><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i></div><p class="small">One lysate per tube<br>Three assay aliquots each</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="0">The three aliquots are technical triplicates of one lysate — not replicates of the biology.</p>
<p class="fine">V = vehicle (0.1% DMSO). Q = compound Q, a selective kinase Q inhibitor (10 µM in 0.1% DMSO). Harvest after 24 h. Assay: kinase Q activity (U/mg protein).</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:06–00:09 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** First trace one culture preparation and its two tubes. Random assignment chooses which tube receives vehicle and which receives Q. The material is harvested after 24 hours. Ask where repeated measurements might enter. Then reveal the assay branch: each tube provides one lysate, assayed in three aliquots — technical triplicates, a detail the opening report did not even mention. Stop at this one preparation. Do not yet reveal how the six “replicates” were generated, the total counts or the day layout.

**Conceptual point:** Trace one piece of biological material through assignment and measurement before counting all repetitions.

**Likely misconception:** Three assay aliquots are three separately treated cultures. In this protocol they all originate from one treated tube.

**Optional follow-up:** Which earlier step would all three aliquots share?

**Sources:** A pp. 73–74, 121–122; R pp. 4–8, 13; D pp. 5–7. Explicit provenance resolves the ambiguity flagged in CONTENT_MAP.md.
:::

## What is N here? {#what-is-n .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Trace the design, then discuss · 2 minutes</p>
<p class="medium">Six separately initiated preparations of L1.<br>Each follows the split we just saw.</p>
<p class="takeaway">What would you count, and what would you call it?</p>
<div class="count-grid fragment">
<div><div class="count">36</div><div class="count-label">assay readings</div></div>
<div><div class="count">12</div><div class="count-label">treatment-assigned tubes</div></div>
<div><div class="count">6</div><div class="count-label">paired biological comparisons</div></div>
</div>

::: notes
**Time: 00:09–00:16 (7 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal that the same split was repeated with six cultures initiated and maintained separately, all from L1. Allow two minutes to draw the hierarchy and decide on counts. Spend three minutes hearing explanations before revealing the 36/12/6 answer. Use two further minutes to ask what each number counts. Each preparation contributes a vehicle-versus-Q comparison. Do not announce that the six comparisons must be independent; we have not yet inspected what they share across days. Ask for a report with nouns, not a bare N.

**Conceptual point:** The number depends on the unit. Twelve assigned tubes form six paired biological comparisons, with 36 assay readings.

**Likely misconception:** The largest count is the biological sample size, or separate preparation labels alone establish independence. The replication and shared-variation discussion follows.

**Optional follow-up:** What claim does this experiment permit if the 36 measurements come from only these six preparations?

**Sources:** A pp. 69, 73–74, 121–122. Combines the previous N question and count-answer slides; discussion is retained.
:::

## How many data points do we really have? {#data-points-concept}

<p class="medium">Treat all 36 readings as separate biological evidence<br>and your analysis looks far more certain than it is.</p>
<div class="research-paths fragment">
<div><h3>Technical replicates</h3><p>3 aliquots of one lysate<br>→ how precise is the assay?</p></div>
<div><h3>Biological replicates</h3><p>6 separately initiated preparations<br>→ how does the biology vary?</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The number of measurements and the amount of evidence are not the same thing.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:16–00:19 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Start from the counts just revealed. If someone analysed all 36 readings as 36 separate biological observations, the analysis would look very precise — narrow uncertainty, confident conclusions — but that precision would be false. Ask why before revealing the two columns. Three aliquots from one lysate share the same cells, treatment and extraction: if that lysate was over-diluted, all three shift together. They tell us how precise the assay is, not how the biology varies. The six separately initiated preparations are the biological replicates; they carry the evidence about compound Q. Neither kind of repetition is useless — they answer different questions. Treating technical replicates as biological ones has a name, pseudoreplication, and it is common in the literature. The exercise on the next slide asks which observations really are independent.

**Conceptual point:** What was repeated determines what the repetition tells you. Technical replicates measure the assay; biological replicates measure the biology.

**Likely misconception:** More measurements always mean more evidence. They do — about the thing that was repeated.

**Optional follow-up:** Which repeat would address an inconsistent plate reader? Which would address inconsistent culture responses?

**Sources:** Lazic (2010) *BMC Neurosci* 11:5 — pseudoreplication; A pp. 12, 68, 73–74, 121–122; R p. 53.
:::

## Which observations are independent? {#independence .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which pairs share a source of variation?</p>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">A</span><span>Two readings</span><span>from one lysate</span></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">B</span><span>Vehicle and compound</span><span>from one preparation</span></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">C</span><span>Two preparations</span><span>measured on the same day</span></div>

::: notes
**Time: 00:19–00:22 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Use one minute of pair discussion and two minutes of debrief. A shares a lysate; B shares its preparation and possibly day; C can share day conditions. Do not simply label C independent. Independence is about the process and model, not the distance between dots or their different identifiers. For C, introduce only that some preparations were measured on the same day. The next slide reveals the full day layout. No numerical plot is needed: the shared sources follow from the experimental history.

**Conceptual point:** Shared sources of variation can make outcomes dependent. Independent technical measurement errors do not turn shared biological material into independent treatment evidence.

**Likely misconception:** Different wells or different labels ensure independence, or a statistical test can certify independence from a small dataset.

**Optional follow-up:** What change to the day's reagents might move several values together?

**Sources:** A pp. 17, 119, 121–122; R pp. 8, 33, 53. The exercise completes the hierarchy discussion without a formal dependence model.
:::

## A paired design {#day-layout}

<div class="day-grid" role="img" aria-label="Actual layout. Day 1 contains preparation pairs P1 and P2. Day 2 contains P3 and P4. Day 3 contains P5 and P6. Every preparation has a vehicle and a compound tube.">
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Day 1</p><div class="pair-row"><span>P1</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div><div class="pair-row"><span>P2</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div></div>
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Day 2</p><div class="pair-row"><span>P3</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div><div class="pair-row"><span>P4</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div></div>
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Day 3</p><div class="pair-row"><span>P5</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div><div class="pair-row"><span>P6</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div></div>
</div>
<div class="legend"><span><i class="dot"></i>Vehicle tube</span><span><i class="tri"></i>Compound tube</span></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Each preparation is its own control: comparing within it cancels what both tubes share.</p>

<!-- REVIEW: Six independent pair contrasts are a teaching-model assumption, not an empirical finding. A day-specific treatment response would induce dependence between the two contrasts on that day. Retain this qualification when editing. -->
::: notes
**Time: 00:22–00:25 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** This is the final notebook reveal: two preparations on each day, and both conditions — vehicle and Q — in every preparation. Name it: this is a paired design. Each preparation provides its own control. Ask the audience to trace one within-day comparison. A change in conditions between days is a batch effect. If a day adds the same amount to both conditions, subtraction removes that component. Ask what happens if Q's response itself differs by day.

**Conceptual point:** The layout separates treatment from day. Pairing can remove a shared additive shift, but does not eliminate all possible batch effects.

**Likely misconception:** Six contrasts are universally independent, or blocking removes every batch problem. The simulation assumes independent preparation effects and technical errors, fixed shared additive day shifts, and no day-by-treatment interaction. A shared treatment response by day could correlate the two contrasts on that day. Independence would then need a different model or more independent days.

**Optional follow-up:** If the compound degrades on one day, will the difference still be unaffected?

**Sources:** A pp. 190–192; R pp. 8, 62. The universal “ideal design” claims in the sources are deliberately not reused. Keep the arithmetic illustration to words; the model details remain in notes.
:::

## What if controls ran on Monday? {#confounding .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Find the missing comparison · with a neighbour, 1 minute</p>
<p class="eyebrow">A different, hypothetical layout</p>
<div class="day-grid fault" role="img" aria-label="Hypothetical confounded design: all vehicle tubes on Monday, all compound tubes on Tuesday, with no within-day treatment comparison.">
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Monday</p><div class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i></div><p>All vehicle tubes</p></div>
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Tuesday</p><div class="pair-mark"><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i></div><p>All compound tubes</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Treatment and day change together. Which caused the difference?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:25–00:28 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Explicitly announce that this is not our actual protocol. It is a hypothetical scheduling shortcut. Give pairs time to identify the missing comparison. Without within-day treatment comparisons, a difference could arise from treatment, day, or both. Label this confounding only after the audience explains the problem. Give the layout comparison its full three minutes. Close the first section with “What claim does this experiment permit?” A treatment-specific claim cannot be separated from a day effect in this alternative layout.

**Conceptual point:** Complete treatment/day confounding prevents separating their effects from these observations alone. More readings of the same lysates do not create the missing comparison.

**Likely misconception:** A later calculation can recover both effects without new information or strong external assumptions. Also avoid suggesting that every batch effect is complete confounding.

**Optional follow-up:** What is the smallest change to the schedule that creates a treatment comparison within a day?

**Sources:** R pp. 6–8, 59–62; A pp. 187–192. New schematic. No questionable numerical claims imported.
:::
